extracted.intended_audience: politically engaged English public / readers of 18th-century political pamphlets
extracted.subtask_description: Polemic letters criticizing a minister's conduct and policy (18th-century political pamphlet addressed to the Duke of Grafton and the reading public). Focuses on what makes ministerial conduct and political argument acceptable or blameworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support measures with argument and decency
rubrics_metrics.description: If the measures in which you have been most successful had been supported by any tolerable appearance of argument, I should have thought my time not ill employed in continuing to examine your conduct... but when I see questions of the highest national importance carried, as they have been, and the first principles of the constitution openly violated, without argument or decency, I confess I give up the cause in despair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public measures, especially those affecting constitutional principles, must be justified by plausible argument and conducted with decency; carrying important measures without argument or respect for the public's understanding is indefensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide plausible pretences when invading rights
rubrics_metrics.description: In former times, the most venal parliaments made it a condition, in their bargain with the minister, that he should furnish them with some plausible pretences for selling their country and themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even corrupt or unpopular measures were historically accompanied by plausible justifications; to take people's rights openly without even plausible reasons is to insult their understanding and is politically reckless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address both passions and understanding (not merely 'to the touch')
rubrics_metrics.description: You neither address yourself to the passions nor the understanding, but simply to the touch. You apply yourself immediately to the feelings of your friends; who, contrary to the forms of parliament, never enter heartily into a debate until they have divided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective political persuasion should engage both reason and sentiment; relying solely on crude appeals to base loyalties or immediate feeling (the 'touch') is poor strategy and demeaning to public debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ministers should possess abilities, integrity, fidelity, and firmness
rubrics_metrics.description: If not the abilities of a great minister, if not the integrity of a patriot, or the fidelity of a friend, show us, at least, the firmness of a man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A minister is to be judged by concrete virtues: competency (abilities), honesty (integrity), patriotic motive (fidelity), and personal courage/steadfastness (firmness). Lacking these traits is a foundational failure of office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of political principle
rubrics_metrics.description: There is something in both which distinguishes you... the first uniform principle, or, if I may call it, the genius of your life, should have carried you through every possible change and contradiction of conduct, without the momentary imputation or colour of a virtue... the wildest spirit of inconsistency should never once have betrayed you into a wise or honourable action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent and self-serving reversals of position (deserting patrons, adopting opposing policies) are a mark of unfitness; ministers should exhibit stable principles rather than pendulous, opportunistic shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citizens' duty is paramount to other engagements
rubrics_metrics.description: They know, that their first duty, as citizens, is paramount to all subsequent engagements: nor will they prefer the discipline, or even the honours of their profession, to those sacred original rights which belonged to them before they were soldiers, and which they claim and possess as the birth-right of Englishmen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating public conduct or mobilizing support, the preservation of constitutional and civic rights must take precedence over professional discipline, honours, or secondary obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public decorum outweighs private vice
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not that he kept a mistress at home, but that he constantly attended her abroad... It is not the private indulgence, but the public insult, of which I complain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private moral failings may be tolerated, but public acts that outrage decorum and insult the public (displaying a mistress in public, humiliating institutions) are politically and socially condemnable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political argument must be built on verifiable facts; truth outranks eloquence
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer, who builds his arguments upon facts such as these, is not easily to be confuted. ... He may want eloquence to amuse and persuade; but, speaking truth, he must always convince.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In political writing and persuasion, grounding claims in verifiable facts is decisive; polished rhetoric cannot substitute for truth. General assertions and reproaches are insufficient against fact-based argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign policy requires dignity and firmness
rubrics_metrics.description: If, instead of disowning lord Shelburne, the British court had interposed with dignity and firmness, you know, my lord, that Corsica would never have been invaded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prevent foreign encroachment, the state must act with clear, dignified resolve; hesitant or distracted policy invites foreign powers to take advantage and may force more costly measures later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiscal responsibility and proper prioritization of public funds
rubrics_metrics.description: I am not versed in the politics of the north; but this, I believe, is certain; that half the money you have distributed to carry the expulsion of Mr. Wilkes, or even your secretary's share in the last subscription, would have kept the Turks at your devotion. Was it economy my lord? or did the coy resistance you have constantly met with in the British senate make you despair of corrupting the divan?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public money should serve clear national interests rather than partisan uses or personal patronage; wasteful or partisan expenditures are open to criticism and can have strategic costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: The historian's duty is to punish by record
rubrics_metrics.description: The condition of the present times is desperate indeed; but there is a debt due to those who come after us; and it is the historian's office to punish, though he cannot correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing historical conduct, the act of recording and exposing misconduct serves as moral punishment and deterrent even where correction is impossible; chronicling failures is a legitimate public duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creating unaccountable power through private networks
rubrics_metrics.description: The interval is carefully employed in forming connexions, creating interests, collecting a party, and laying the foundation of double marriages; until the deluded prince... finds him, at last, too strong to be commanded, and too formidable to be removed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Building private patronage networks, interests, and interlocking alliances risks producing a ministerial power that evades accountability; such practices are politically dangerous and condemnable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not deceive the sovereign with false reports of public temper
rubrics_metrics.description: You may continue to deceive your gracious master with false representations of the temper and condition of his subjects: you may command a venal vote... but never hope that the freeholders will make a tame surrender of their rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ministers and advisers owe truthful representations of public sentiment to the sovereign; manipulating or misrepresenting the people's condition to the monarch is dishonest and risks grave consequences for the constitution.
